q2_walk_forward_2025.note: higher is better; weights from 2023-24 skill only

q2_same_population_check.why: TOP10 covers 370 of FLAT's 486 players; raw comparison confounds weighting with coverage. Re-scored both on exactly TOP10's 370.
q2_same_population_check.verdict: TOP10 loses narrowly on identical players (-0.009); the larger raw gap was population, not weighting.

headline: Q1: expert skill PERSISTS (rho 0.276 and 0.367, both clear the 400-shuffle null p95). Q2: it is too weak to exploit — CONTINUOUS ties FLAT (+0.002), TOP10 loses on same players (-0.009) and costs 24% coverage. The flat ~200-expert consensus is effectively optimal as a mean anchor.

q3_slices_run_2026-08-18.method: same skill score and 200-draw shuffle null as Q1, restricted per slice; min_common 15 (positions) / 10 (rookies); rookie slice approximates years_exp-as-of-season from current years_exp (2026 - season)
q3_slices_run_2026-08-18.verdict: Cory's theory is STRUCTURALLY RIGHT: expert skill is position-specific — RB skill persists strongest (rho .47/.27), WR persists, rookie-evaluation skill persists both transitions (.19/.32), TE is borderline, and QB skill does NOT persist at all (slightly negative — every 'QB guru' is luck at this sample). BUT it is still not exploitable by re-weighting: even in the strongest slices the skill-weighted consensus ties FLAT walk-forward (RB 0.7837 vs 0.7848; rookies identical). The crowd average already contains the specialists. Actionable residue: never pay for a single expert's QB takes, and the rookie-skill persistence licenses a post-draft study on whether the TOP rookie evaluators' DISAGREEMENT (not their average) flags rookie busts/breakouts.
